normalization_decisions.rule: Canal name verbatim per master 'Notable ship canals' table row labels. 11 closed values: Saint Lawrence Seaway / White Sea–Baltic Canal / Suez Canal / Rhine–Main–Danube Canal / Volga–Don Canal / Kiel Canal / Houston Ship Channel / Panama Canal / Danube–Black Sea Canal / Manchester Ship Canal / Welland Canal. Note en-dash characters ('–' not '-') in multi-name canals: 'White Sea–Baltic', 'Rhine–Main–Danube', 'Volga–Don', 'Danube–Black Sea'. 'Houston Ship Channel' (NOT 'Houston Canal' — Wikipedia article + master use 'Ship Channel'). 'Saint Lawrence Seaway' (compound waterway — included per master).

Integer year of opening per master table. For canals with multiple historical versions (Welland Canal: First 1829, Second 1845, Third 1887, Fourth 1932), master uses current-canal version (Welland = 1932 for Fourth Welland Canal). All staged Year Opened values per cycle-1 audit's verbatim dump.

Numeric length in kilometers per master table. Range: 600 km (Saint Lawrence Seaway, longest compound waterway) → 43.4 km (Welland Canal, shortest in master — clears 10-row gate). Decimal precision varies per master: most are integers, two are 1-decimal (193.3 Suez; 64.4 Danube–Black Sea; 43.4 Welland).

Text in compound format 'length x beam x draft' per master cell convention (e.g., '226 x 24 x 8' for Saint Lawrence Seaway = max ship dimensions 226m length × 24m beam × 8m draft). Suez Canal has 'Unlimited x 78 x 20' = no length limit (only beam + draft constraints). Houston Ship Channel '305 x 161 x 14' (note: 161m beam reflects the wide channel; some sources interpret differently). Preserved verbatim per master cell.

Text in format 'Country: Start point — Country: End point' per master cell convention, with em-dash separator '—' (NOT hyphen). For single-country canals: 'Russia: Lake Onega — White Sea in Belomorsk' (one country prefix, then continuation phrasing). For Panama Canal: 'Panama: Caribbean — Pacific Ocean' (oceanic endpoints). For Suez Canal: 'Egypt: Port Said — Port Tewfik' (two ports). For Saint Lawrence Seaway: 'Canada: Port Colborne — Canada: Montreal' (both endpoints in same country). Country prefix convention follows master.

open_questions.question: Why does the Saint Lawrence Seaway show 600 km when it's a compound waterway (river + canals + locks)?
open_questions.answer: Per cycle-1 audit's master dump: Wikipedia's Ship canal article includes Saint Lawrence Seaway in 'Notable ship canals' table with 600 km length representing the navigable channel from Port Colborne (Lake Erie) to Montreal. The Seaway is a compound waterway including the Welland Canal + parts of the St. Lawrence River + multiple locks; master treats it as one entry.

open_questions.question: Why is the Grand Canal of China (1776 km, ancient) NOT in this instance despite being the world's longest canal?
open_questions.answer: Per cycle-1 audit's master-derived dump: Wikipedia's 'Ship canal' article's 'Notable ship canals' table does NOT include the Grand Canal of China. The Grand Canal is in other Wikipedia lists ('List of canals', UNESCO World Heritage Sites) but the strict-master-table universe for this instance excludes it. The 'Ship canal' article's curated 'Notable ship canals' table appears to focus on modern industrial-era ship canals; the ancient Grand Canal (~600 CE) may be classified differently in Wikipedia's canal categorization.

open_questions.question: Why is Welland Canal Year Opened = 1932 instead of 1829 (original)?
open_questions.answer: Per cycle-1 audit master dump: Wikipedia master uses the Fourth Welland Canal opening year (1932) which is the current operational canal. The First Welland Canal opened 1829; rebuilt 1845 (Second), 1887 (Third), 1932 (Fourth/current). Master's current-canal convention used.

open_questions.question: What about the Erie Canal, Rideau Canal, Caledonian Canal — why excluded?
open_questions.answer: Per cycle-1 audit: those canals are NOT in Wikipedia's 'Ship canal' article 'Notable ship canals' table. Erie Canal (584 km, 1825) is famous historically but the master table excludes it — possibly because it's no longer used for ship transit and is now primarily heritage/recreational. Rideau Canal (Canada, 1832) is UNESCO World Heritage but not in master 'Notable ship canals' table. Caledonian Canal (Scotland, 1822) similarly excluded. Strict-master-table policy preserves source_defined cleanly.

open_questions.question: Why is Houston Ship Channel included alongside major international canals like Suez/Panama?
open_questions.answer: Per cycle-1 audit's master-derived dump: Wikipedia's 'Ship canal' article's 'Notable ship canals' table includes Houston Ship Channel (80 km, opened 1914 — same year as Panama Canal coincidentally) reflecting its status as one of the busiest US ship channels handling significant ocean-going traffic. The 'notable' framing in master title encompasses ship-channel infrastructure broadly, not just international/iconic canals.
